Laghu हारीत Smṛti
------------------------------------------
During the ancient and medieval times, the life of a Hindu was well-regulated, both at the personal and at the social levels, by the धर्मशास्त्रस्. As time passed and social changes became inevitable, newer धर्मशास्त्रस् or revised editions of the older ones appeared on the scene, composed by competent scholars who had realised the need for such changes. Such works were generally preceded by the words ‘Laghu’ or ‘Vṛddha’, especially when the authors belonged to the particular schools or traditions of the older composers of these works.
The Laghu हारीत Smṛti is one such work. Two versions or editions of the same are available now.
The first one contains seven chapters and 250 verses. The main content of this work deals with the four varṇas, the four āśramas as also योग.
The second version has only 117 verses and deals with śuddhis (purificatory ceremonies), prāyaścittas (expiatory rites), अशौच (ceremonial impurity connected with birth and death), śrāddhas (after-death rites) as also rules about इन्हेरितन्चे and पर्तितिओन्.
See also DHARMAŚĀSTRAS.

Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha
------------------------------------------
The Yogavāsiṣṭha—also known as योगवासिष्ठ Rāmāyaṇa—is a well-known standard treatise dealing with Advaita Vedānta of an uncompromising type. This voluminous work (of 23,734 verses in six prakaraṇas or sections) has been summarised by several writers. One such work more well-known than the others is the Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha attributed to one Abhinanda (9th century A. D.), a ब्राह्मण from Kāśmīra (Kashmir). It has six prakaraṇas or sections, containing 5000 verses.
Only a very brief summary of the same can be given here.
1. Vairāgyaprakaraṇa
(3 chapters, 359 verses)
The work begins in a dramatic setting. Śrī राम goes on a पिल्ग्रिमगे with the permission of his ड़थेर् दशरथ. After returning, he becomes a little dejected and develops intense वैराग्य (spirit of renunciation). As a result he loses all interest in life. Seeing this, the sages who had gathered there under the leadership of विश्वामित्र, request वसिष्ठ to tackle the problem. Then ensues a long dialogue between him and Śrī राम, continuing till the end of the work.
The gist of this section centres round the evanescent nature of the world. Pleasures of life are temporary, ultimately leading to suffering. Everything in this world is destructible. Attachment to it leads to सṁसार (transmigration). मिन्द् is subject to vāsanās (past impressions). Hence attempts should be made to destroy these vāsanās and attain freedom.
2. Mumukṣuvyavahāra prakaraṇa
(one chapter, 110 verses)
This section concentrates on the subject of conquest of vāsanās, deep impressions in the मिन्द् carried over from past lives.
The मिन्द् can be compared to a river flowing in two parallel streams viz., śubhavāsanās (good impressions) and aśubhavāsanās (bad impressions). The mumukṣu (seeker after लिबेरतिओन्) should try to increase the former, and, attenuate and destroy the latter. This is possible only if there is puruṣaprayatna or self-effort.
Mokṣa or लिबेरतिओन् is compared to a mansion with four entrances, each being guarded by a sentry. They are शम (internal peace), विवेक (discrimination), sādhusaṅga (company of holy persons) and सन्तोष (contentment). Out of these, sādhusaṅga is the easiest and the most effective.
3. Utpattiprakaraṇa
(9 chapters, 1008 verses)
This section mainly propagates the advaitic doctrine known as ‘dṛṣṭi-सृष्टि-वाद’ (See DṚṢṬI-सृष्टि-VĀDA for details.).
The whole world is a च्रेअतिओन् of the मिन्द्. If the मिन्द् is stilled, the world that binds, also disappears.
There are some interesting upākhyānas (stories) like Līlopākhyāna, Indropākhyāna, Brāhmaṇopākhyāna and Lavaṇopākhyāna to illustrate the important teachings.
Saptabhūmikās—seven stages of knowledge from śubhecchā upto turyagā—have also been described.
4. Sthitiprakaraṇa
(5 chapters, 541 verses)
Sthiti or sustenance of this world is also an imagination of the मिन्द् like utpatti or च्रेअतिओन्. This is the important teaching of this section.
A person, identified with the body-मिन्द्-complex thinks he is the doer and enjoyer. Hence he gets bound. He can free himself by cultivating one of these two attitudes: ‘I am not the doer,’ ‘I am not the body’; ‘I do everything’, ‘I am every-thing’.
The sādhaka can also free himself by constantly thinking that he is subtler than the subtlest.
There are five interesting stories in this section also.
5. Upaśamaprakaraṇa
(10 chapters, 1124 verses)
The main topic of this section is how to quieten the मिन्द् and lead it to dissolution.
It is due to the मिन्द् that we have the sense of ‘I’, ‘you’ and ‘this’. This can be dissolved by dissolving the मिन्द् (called manonāśa here). At first one has to cultivate good vāsanās or tendencies such as मैत्री (friendly attitude towards all beings), karuṇā (compassion) and so on. Then one has to transcend even these when the मिन्द् as मिन्द् gets dissolved. This leads to a direct awareness of the आत्मन् or the Self.
This section too contains several upākhyānas or stories as those of जनक, बलि, प्रह्लाद, उद्दालक and others.
6. Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa
(18 chapters, 1859 verses)
This long section deals with निर्वाण or मोक्ष (liberation) and the nature of a liberated सोउल्. Through self-effort, the sādhaka gradually destroys all vāsanās and realises his essential nature as ब्रह्मन्. This can be attained only by the pure बुद्धि or intellect. Though śāstra (the scriptures), गुरु (spiritual teacher) and their teachings are a help, they have no direct role to play.
In this section, there are references to जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् as also the Bhagavadgītā. Also, as in other sections there are plenty of stories like those of Bhuśuṇḍa, अर्जुन, भगीरथ, कच and इक्ष्वाकु to illustrate the teachings given here.
On the whole it is an extremely interesting work and can serve as an introduction to the study of the bigger work, the Yogavāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa.

Laghu Viṣṇusmṛti
------------------------------------------
This is a late work of the धर्म-śāstra literature, having five chapters and 114 verses. It deals mainly with the four varṇas and the four āśramas.
Though अपरार्क (12th century A. D.) has quoted a few verses from a Laghu Viṣṇusmṛti in his commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, those verses are not found in the printed texts available now.
See also LAGHU-हारीत-SMṚTI.

laghimā
(‘the power to become light or weightless’)
------------------------------------------
The desire to acquire सिद्धिस् or super-natural powers is not uncommon among the spiritual aspirants. पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his Yogasūtras (3.45) mentions about eight such सिद्धिस् among which लघिमा is also one. It is the power to become extremely light.
Such सिद्धिस् can be obtained by तपस् (austerity) as also mantrajapa (repetition of holy syllables).
Even levitation may result from the attainment of this power.

lāghava
(‘lightness’)
------------------------------------------
An earnest practice of yogic exercises like प्राणायाम (See PRĀṆĀYĀMA for details.) under the guidance of an expert teacher will engender certain signs, both physical and psychical, by which one can judge the progress. One of these is लाघव or laghutva, a feeling of lightness of the body, indicating good health.
See ŚVETĀŚVATARA UPANIṢAD (2.13).

Laghunyāsa
(‘minor-process of placing [various deities on one’s limbs]’)
------------------------------------------
The महान्यास involves the worship of Lord शिव in great detail. (See MAHĀNYĀSA.) When, due to any valid reason the votary cannot perform it, a shorter version of the same called ‘Laghunyāsa’ has been prescribed.
The following are the more important steps involved in this लघुन्यास:
Physical preparations for the worship; preliminary prayer to शिव that helps in fixing the मिन्द् on him; ṛṣyādinyāsa (statement about the ṛṣi or the sage who discovered it, the devatā or the deity and the purpose); placing the various deities like ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, Hara, इन्द्र and others on one’s limbs through imagination with appropriate mantras; āhvāna or inviting the deity शिव to be present to accept the worship; offering the various उपचारस् (modes of direct service) like आसन (seat for sitting), pādya and अर्घ्य (water for washing feet and hands) etc., right up to स्नान or bath; bathing the शिवलिङ्ग with the mantras of the Rudra and Camaka; offering of other items of worship like cloth, flowers, बिल्व leaves, lighted lamp and ड़ोओद्.
One who worships शिव in this way is blessed with many fruits like destruction of sins, gaining wealth and health, attaining longevity, getting children, as also powers of the intellect.
